https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Andy Burnham has paused the early release scheme initiated under his Labour predecessor but still faces pressure to act on prison overcrowding. Photograph: Jack Taylor/PA View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has paused the early release scheme initiated under his Labour predecessor but still faces pressure to act on prison overcrowding. Photograph: Jack Taylor/PA Prisons and probation Burnham to focus on keeping child rapists in prison as release scheme talks enter final day Review goes down to the wire after ministers speak with victims’ representatives and support services Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.27 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham is focused on preventing the release of child sexual abuse perpetrators as part of the government’s early release scheme, as urgent talks on which serious criminals could be exempted go down to the wire. Government ministers are understood to have 24 hours to assess which criminals can be released early to free up prison space, with every exemption weighed up against the threat of the criminal justice system’s collapse. The prime minister halted controversial plans to release thousands of killers, rapists and sex offenders from prison in September, intended to ease critical prison overcrowding, during his second week in the role. He is keen to make as many exceptions as the small headroom in the prison estate will allow, the Guardian understands. Burnham wants to keep child rapists and other perpetrators of serious sexual abuse from being released early after ministers heard the concerns of victims’ representatives and support services who warned that a failure to put in place safeguards for abuse victims would put them at particular risk . A review of the scheme is expected to conclude by the end of Monday to give the Prison Service time to prepare, with a final decision on exemptions still to be made. But ministers are keenly aware that if no action is taken, prisons will run out of space, while exempting some criminals is likely to lead to further calls for others to also be kept behind bars, sources told the Guardian. The former justice secretary David Lammy, who brought forward the act that paved the way for the releases, previously warned that failing to implement it could leave no capacity across jails in England and Wales in November. The new justice secretary, appointed by Burnham on 20 July, is Alex Norris. The early release scheme – accompanied by a significant expansion in electronic tagging of offenders – is still expected to take place this autumn with an initial group of about 700, despite warnings by probation officers of potential chaos . It is likely to cause a headache for the new prime minister as he faces the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, in the House of Commons for the first time. A government source said: “If we don’t take any action, we will run out of room – it’s not sustainable at all.” It comes after the family of PC Andrew Harper expressed outrage that his killers may be eligible for early release. His mother, Debbie Adlam, said the proposed inclusion of two of her son’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – was “another letdown” for their family. View image in fullscreen PC Andrew Harper sustained fatal injuries while responding to a reported burglary in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA New sentencing laws were passed under Keir Starmer’s government to ease a looming prison overcrowding crisis that ministers said could seize up the criminal justice system . Victims’ advocates are concerned that high prisoner numbers will limit the number of serious criminals who could be exempted. The former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips, a vocal critic of the scheme , said it was right that exemptions were being considered but there needed to be “a whole system change with how victims and risk is managed as the sentencing review goes forward”, which had to be carried out with victims’ agencies, probation officers and police. Under the Sentencing Act 2026 , which passed in January, from September some serious offenders will be eligible for release halfway through their sentences rather than two-thirds of the way through. Those convicted of less serious crimes can be freed after serving a third of their sentence instead of 40%. The new law also restricts the use of short-term prison stays, which will be replaced with probation and community orders – a move that some critics have said will put pressure on an already overburdened probation service. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion Will Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy | Simon Jenkins Read more Phillips said any review needed to examine not only the early release scheme but the presumption against short sentences. “Exemptions are an immediate safety crisis, but real in-depth work to make the situation better forever and be one based on risk and rehabilitation must be done,” she said. Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, met Norris on Wednesday, and she told the Telegraph she welcomed his acknowledgment that victims had been let down and she was “cautiously more hopeful” about progress on answering her concerns. But prison reform groups, government officials and politicians reacted angrily to Burnham’s decision to pause the scheme, warning that abandoning measures to ease jail overcrowding could lead to the criminal justice system “collapsing under its own weight”. Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England and Wales, said centres had been supporting scores of victims through the “distress and terror of finding out that their rapists and abusers were due to be released … or in some cases already had been”. She said: “Victim-survivors should never have been put in this situation, not least because so little is known about the factors which make some more like to offend than others, and how sexual violence offenders can effectively be managed and monitored in the community.” A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said it was taking action to fix the prisons crisis, “caused by 14 years of Conservative neglect”. “We are pulling every lever to protect the public and cut crime,” they said, pointing to the building of new prisons, expanding tagging, strengthening community punishment and giving victims a say in offenders’ licence conditions. “We have paused changes due to start in September to conduct an urgent review to make sure we get this policy right for victims without running out of prison spaces.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation UK criminal justice Andy Burnham Labour news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Prisoner early release scheme paused by Andy Burnham may still go ahead Mahmood and Streeting accused of making ‘cheap jokes’ about prisoner early release scheme Expansion of electronic tagging in England and Wales will put public at risk, watchdog warns Ministers warned not to scapegoat prison staff over mistaken release of Hadush Kebatu Education cuts in prisons ultimately endanger the public, watchdog says Robert Jenrick’s call to arm prison officers is ‘nonsense’, governors say Prisons minister vows to end ‘toxic’ cover-up culture in England and Wales Staffordshire prison locked down after third violent incident in weeks UK prison officers to demand electric stun guns for dangerous jails Ban inmates from cooking after Hashem Abedi assault, says prison union Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

By Kevin Hyland & Robert D. Marin

In 2016, then-Prime Minister Theresa May marked the first anniversary of the United Kingdom’s Modern Slavery Act with a commentary touting how our research in the UK and Romania had helped uncover “criminal gangs creating twinned towns of modern slavery.” What made our approach unique was the pairing of specific source and destination localities as a single unit of analysis. Despite this prominent endorsement, our twinning methodology for understanding modern slavery was not further developed as a policy tool. A decade later, its absence undermines the global fight against modern slavery and human trafficking, because linking places of origin and destination is a better guide for official intervention than a purely national approach.

Trafficking is mostly framed as a macro phenomenon driven by asymmetries between rich and poor regions. While this framing identifies important structural causes, it does not fully explain how these networks operate. Instead of following Romanian population patterns in the UK, as one might expect, our research shows a more specific geography of recruitment and exploitation in cases of trafficking and modern slavery.

As Tim Hall of the University of Winchester has argued, macro-level explanations obscure the localized aspects of organized crime. Criminals base their business models on the opportunities available where they live. Moreover, localities are not bounded containers, but nodes that are formed through wider social relations. A Romanian county, for example, becomes a trafficking hub because recruitment networks, migration cycles, and destination-side demand sustain links to particular places that enable and encourage the growth of criminal networks.

This illustrates the late sociologist Ronald Robertson's concept of glocalization: globalization operates through localized differentiation, reinforcing rather than dissolving the individuality of local settings. Criminal networks exploit local settings by embedding themselves in the specific source and destination localities of cross-border slavery and trafficking corridors, connecting the two. These recurrent pairs are produced by migration histories and demand for labour and sexual exploitation. The structural inequalities between source and destination localities condition these corridors, which can be partly revealed by governmental efforts to disrupt or contain them. Thus, twinning differs from “transnational trafficking” or “cross-border organized crime”—terms that describe a category of criminal activity rather than the relational structure that sustains it.

We observed such twinning between 2011 and 2023, when overseeing Romanian National Police secondments to UK police forces. Working together, the officers documented 55 Romanian-UK trafficking cases in which both the source county and the destination region were identified. Of the resulting 88 county-to-region pairings, 30 route to Greater London, while on the Romanian side, Dâmbovița appears in 12 cases, Ilfov in 11, Buzău in 10, and Brăila in nine. This is, of course, hardly an exhaustive mapping of the criminal geography in both countries.

At the same time, several Romanian counties link to different UK regions simultaneously. This reflects the mobility of trafficking networks themselves and supports previous findings that Romanian origin-destination profiles are not always geographically contiguous.

Once such criminal twinning is identified, how should policymakers respond? Action at only one end will always be incomplete. A bilateral and multi-domain policy, one that ties prevention in the source jurisdiction with demand reduction in the destination jurisdiction, is essential.

When May referred to the “twinned towns of modern slavery” in 2016, she named a pattern that researchers had started to document. Since then, the evidence has further supported this interpretation, suggesting that the concept offers a stronger basis for organizing policy responses to modern slavery and human trafficking than national aggregates or isolated interventions do.

Unfortunately, the many official and civil-society actors trying to address these patterns often do not see themselves as part of the same operation. Our twinning framework provides a shared roadmap that promises to strengthen their efforts, without requiring the creation of new agencies, powers, or agreements. It directs resources to the specific pairs of places where trafficking concentrates, so that prevention campaigns can target the source localities feeding a particular destination. Local authorities and police forces can then cooperate as pairs, diaspora organizations can act as protection intermediaries within their own corridor, and results can be measured corridor by corridor rather than lost in national totals.

Kevin Hyland is the UK's first Anti-Slavery Commissioner and CEO of Praeveni Global, a nonprofit focused on preventing modern slavery and human trafficking. Robert D. Marin, a former secretary of state in the Romanian Ministry of Internal Affairs, is a doctoral researcher at the University of Nottingham—the Rights Lab.

https://www.citizen.co.za/news/news-worl.text: World Home » News » World Czech minister’s body exhumed to resolve doubts over 1948 death By Agence France Presse 2 minute read 2 September 2026 03:31 pm RELATED ARTICLES ‘We are deeply saddened’: Transport department and Santaco respond after 2 crashes claim 28 lives Ratile Mabitsela opens up about suicide attempt and husband’s suicide The Czech Republic has reopened the Jan Masaryk case after new intelligence records emerged from the US, Britain and France. Former pro-Western Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk’s body was found on March 10, 1948 under the window of his official apartment and the authorities shelved the case as a suicide. Picture: AFP Add as Preferred Source on Google Follow on Google News Czech police on Wednesday started exhuming the remains of former pro-Western Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk, who died under suspicious circumstances shortly after a 1948 communist coup, they said. Masaryk’s body was found on March 10, 1948 under the window of his official apartment and the authorities shelved the case as a suicide, but questions have remained. Police reopen decades-old mystery The Office for the Documentation and the Investigation of the Crimes of Communism, a unit of Czech police, is now investigating the case as a suspected murder. Police said on X they had started exhuming the body at a cemetery near the presidential summer residence of Lany, west of Prague early on Wednesday. “We believe this will help us clarify the circumstances behind the death of Jan Masaryk,” said police. Read more ‘It is a scourge’: Santaco calls for collective response to Gauteng women’s deaths Police spokesman Jakub Vincalek told AFP that police would try to complete the examination of the body “as fast as possible” but declined to give details. New evidence prompts fresh investigation Police have reviewed the case several times since the communist government was toppled in the Velvet Revolution of 1989, four years before Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. They announced they would review Masaryk’s death in early 2025, following the discovery of new diplomatic and intelligence records from the United States, Britain and France. Masaryk, the son of Czechoslovakia’s first president Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, was foreign minister in the Czechoslovak exile government in London during World War II and kept the job after the war. He declined to join mass resignations of non-communist ministers that paved the way to power for the Moscow-backed government in February 1948. Photo: Annie Spratt / unsplash.com Leyla Cheamil , 07.09.2026, 14:00 The long-awaited summer holiday has come to an end, and after about two and a half months, Romanian students returned to school on Monday. A new school year lies ahead, filled with excitement, hopes, successes, and disappointments. In school hallways, the bell rings once again, signaling the start of classes as millions of students embark on a new journey full of challenges, one in which they will gain new knowledge, learn to think critically, collaborate with classmates, and express their creativity. Teachers, who have prepared for the new school year, are also reliving the joy of reuniting with their students and the curiosity of getting to know those who are crossing the school threshold for the first time. Education requires responsible measures based on data and the evaluation of results, and any reform must be supported by dialogue, resources, and time to be effective, President Nicuşor Dan stated in a message marking the start of the 2026–2027 school year. The head of state emphasized that education is not limited to grades, gradebook, or exams, but it also encompasses “the trust a teacher places in a student, a parent’s patience, and a child’s courage to ask questions, make mistakes, and try again.” Nicuşor Dan also highlighted the role of schools in shaping adults capable of critical thinking, a mission that is “more challenging than ever.” In his turn, the Acting Education Minister Mihai Dimian urged students in a message to cherish the opportunity to learn, emphasizing that education is the key that opens the door to the world for them. Mihai Dimian also told his fellow educators and teachers that they bear “a great responsibility—the destiny of these children.” The new school year brings national assessment standards for students who have now started first grade. And those admitted to high school this summer are in for a change: they will be learning according to new curriculum frameworks. The Acting Education Minister Mihai Dimian estimates that they will be able to use the printed textbooks in the second half of next month and the digital ones starting this month. On the other hand, education union leaders are sounding the alarm, stating that the school year is starting with major problems: teachers who don’t know if they’ll be able to meet their teaching load, and too many unqualified teachers in the classroom. Union representatives say that, at this time, there are teachers who are still looking for classes to fill out their teaching load. Teachers in pre-university education who are paid on an hourly basis are also facing problems, as they will be subject to a new, lower hourly rate than before. This is a direct result of a government decision enacted this year regarding the national minimum wage. Union representatives say that education must be given the social priority it deserves, and, regarding a future salary law, they will not accept anything less than what has already been negotiated. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/04/bosn.text: Polls opened Sunday in Bosnia's general election, where some 3.4 million voters are choosing the three members of the multi-ethnic presidency, national lawmakers, and leaders of the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.The complex system of institutions was created by the US-brokered 1995 peace agreement to manage divisions among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.Early reports show voting was delayed at several polling places due to problems with new digital voting technology, which was introduced to address earlier concerns about vote tampering. Polls close at 7 pm. local time.The election comes as many citizens in the multiethnic Balkan state face everyday problems, while some leading politicians stoke the war-era tensions that have kept the country divided since the 1992-95 conflict.New election security measuresFor the first time, authorities are using electronic voter identification and ballot scanning to curb the irregularities and organised manipulation that undermined confidence in earlier elections.Most of the 75 parties running are organised along ethnic lines. The Bosniak nationalist Party of Democratic Action has campaigned on keeping Bosnia united against Serb separatism, while many Bosnian Croats back ethnic parties such as the local branch of Croatia's ruling Croatian Democratic Union.Izetbegovic, who was beaten by Becirovic in 2022, is seeking a third term as president of the centre-right SDA, the largest Bosniak party in the nation.Many disillusioned citizens say politicians use nationalism to avoid tackling real problems like low living standards and the exodus of young people. Mostar voter Ivan Silic said nothing has improved since he first voted and that politicians live well while everyone else's situation stays the same.Dodik looms large despite not being on the ballotDespite not being on the ballot, the campaign has been dominated by Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian, separatist former president of Republika Srpska. Dodik is banned from public office after being convicted of defying the international envoy who oversees the peace agreement.Fresh from meeting Russia's president Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Dodik leads a party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, that is likely to win in Republika Srpska.At a final rally Friday in Banja Luka, attended by Russia's ambassador, Igor Khalabukov, Dodik declared Bosnia is "dead" and "an impossible country". "It doesn't make any sense," he stressed.Off the ballot for the first time in almost 30 years, he is still in command and is present across the country's media, says Dragan Bursac, an analyst. In Bursac's view, the ban is not working, and Dodik is exploiting it.Ethnic tensions continue to riseBosnia has been peaceful in recent years, but its politicians have kept ethnic divisions alive. Bosnian Serb leaders such as Dodik have pushed for their entity to break away, raising Western fears of renewed instability.The Balkan nation remains one of Europe's poorest countries, still recovering from a war that began after it declared independence from Serb-led Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state. That conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.The country is formally seeking European Union membership, but progress has stalled despite EU efforts to push its leaders toward reform.Major powers continue to influence socio-economic and political life in the small Balkan nation. Russia is holding down the EU's efforts to expand its membership throughout the Balkans, including Bosnia, while continuing to back the Republika Srpska.While a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas is being pushed by a corporation with ties to the Trump administration as part of the US's efforts to gain influence.And recently, wartime wounds were reopened by public tributes in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to Ratko Mladic, the wartime army commander who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.Bosnian Serbs regard him as a hero, despite his UN court conviction over the killing of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995.Senior Bosnian Serb officials attended his funeral in Belgrade, drawing sharp EU criticism and angering Bosniak politicians.

https://www.thepinknews.com/2026/09/30/e.text: Crime Netflix ‘Manosphere’ streamer Ed Matthews fined for lewd comment to female shop worker Sep 30 Written by Jack Wetherill Share Save for later Comment Ed Matthews appeared on Louis Theroux’s Netflix documentary (Netflix) ‘ Manosphere ‘ streamer Ed Matthews, who appeared in Louis Theroux’s Netflix documentary Inside the Manosphere , has been fined £4,500 after pleading guilty to making lewd sexual remarks to a Sainsbury’s worker in Lancaster. The 24-year-old was fined £2,884 and ordered to pay a £1,154 victim surcharge, £85 in costs and £500 in compensation. The court heard the incident happened on 2 March at around 9pm, when the worker was cleaning near the alcohol aisle and a group of five men approached her. As per the The Sun , prosecutor Mr Anderton told the court: “Mr Matthews asked her about Yorkshire puddings and then asked whether she liked English wood.” Queer News. Straight Up. The LGBTQ+ stories you don’t want to miss, delivered to your inbox daily. Thanks for registering! You can update your email subscriptions at any time in the My profile section of your account. Matthews then asked the worker, who “knew this meant penis” whether she was a lesbian after she said she did not like “Polish wood”. Mr Anderton said the worker felt trapped because the men had surrounded her, and that she felt sexualised and uncomfortable during the exchange. The court heard she gave one of the men her Instagram details to get rid of the group, before reporting what had happened to her manager. What happened The exchange was described in court as a sustained incident, rather than a brief comment in passing. Chair magistrate Deborah Topping said: “It wasn’t just one or two words and then you walked away – it was sustained.” The court also heard Matthews was on crutches at the time, while the worker had her arm in a sling due to a shoulder injury. Matthews pleaded guilty to one charge of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress. Turning to religion According to Matthews’ lawyer Mr Rathor, the social media star regretted his actions and had turned a new leaf after time in HMP Chelmsford earlier in the year. “Since his release from prison he has been delivering a new message,” Mr Rathor said. “The two weeks spent in HMP Chelmsford made him turn over a new leaf. He’s turned to God and he wants to inspire the young.” Inside the Manosphere Matthews is part of the UK’s online “manosphere” ecosystem, a loose network of controversial creators and communities built around hyper-masculine, often misogynistic talking points. Louis Theroux’s Inside the Manosphere helped push those online dynamics into the mainstream.
